hero.title: Privacy
meta.title: Privacy | Speak Away
meta.description: Learn how Speak Away handles dictation, meeting notes and your data on your device. Read about local storage, permissions and your privacy controls.
summary.title: Summary
summary.sent: Nothing you say or type is sent to us.
stored.title: What stays on your device
stored.history: History is on by default and stays on your Mac. It saves final and raw dictated text, the app name, the date and the word count, up to 2,000 entries. You can turn it off and delete entries one by one.
stored.notes: Meeting notes are saved as <date> <title>.md, with a .json beside each note for the app, in ~/Library/Application Support/Speak Away/Meetings/. A temporary live journal of the transcript is kept during a meeting and deleted when the note is saved. If the note cannot be saved, or the app is interrupted, the journal stays in that folder until your next meeting replaces it. The note has no summary until you press “Resumir” (Summarize).
stored.other: Stats are plain counters. Your scratchpad, dictionary, voice shortcuts, writing styles and settings also stay on your Mac. Audio is never written to storage.
stored.processing: Whisper processes dictation on your Mac. Filler-word cleanup is rule based, runs on your Mac and is on by default. Meeting summaries, the optional “Pulir con Apple Intelligence” polish (Polish with Apple Intelligence, off by default) and Command Mode use Apple’s on-device model and need macOS 26 with Apple Intelligence. Dictation and filler-word cleanup do not.
network.title: What leaves your device
network.mac: The Mac app’s only network requests go to Hugging Face, through WhisperKit: the model download, about 632 MB (precise, default) or 216 MB (fast), and small tokenizer files when they are not cached. The default model downloads when you first open the app, and the other one the first time you pick it. A model downloads again only if its folder on your Mac is missing or incomplete. Hugging Face sees these requests as any website would. Dictation works offline after the download.
network.iphone: On iPhone, speech recognition uses Apple’s own on-device recognition assets. Apple supplies those assets; they may need to be downloaded.
network.copy: The app’s “Copiar para ChatGPT” button (Copy for ChatGPT) copies meeting notes as a ready to paste prompt. It does not send them. If you paste them into ChatGPT or Claude yourself, you are choosing to share them there.
permissions.title: Permissions and why
permissions.mic.text: On Mac, to hear you during dictation and meetings.
permissions.audio.text: On Mac, to capture the sound your Mac plays separately from your microphone. This includes the other side of a call and any music or video, except Speak Away’s own sound, so those can end up in the transcript. On macOS 14.0 to 14.3, or if that method cannot start, Speak Away falls back to macOS screen capture, which it uses only for the sound: it discards the video frames, and macOS asks for screen recording permission instead.
permissions.input.text: On Mac, to notice the Fn key. The listener sees key events but reads only the key code and modifier flags, never what you type.
permissions.access.text: On Mac, to paste text where your cursor is, to keep the Fn key from reaching other apps, and for Command Mode to press the copy shortcut that reads your selection.
permissions.iphone.text: To hear your voice and transcribe it with Apple’s on-device speech recognition.
clipboard.title: Clipboard
clipboard.text: To paste, Speak Away first puts the dictated text on the system clipboard, where other apps, including clipboard managers, can read it. With Accessibility permission, it then pastes at your cursor and tries to put back what you had copied, unless you copied something else in between. In some cases the dictated text can stay on the clipboard until you copy something else. Without Accessibility, Speak Away cannot paste for you. Command Mode reads your selected text through the clipboard so it can rewrite that selection from your spoken instruction: it presses the copy shortcut for you, reads what lands on the clipboard and then puts back what you had copied.
iphone.title: iPhone: app and keyboard
iphone.text: The iPhone app and keyboard are available on the App Store. The app uses Apple’s on-device speech recognition. When you start a session, the app keeps the microphone running in the background for the length you pick (5 minutes, 15 minutes, 1 hour or until you stop it) so the keyboard can start dictation. Between dictations, the app drops every sound it hears, without storing or measuring it, and iOS shows its microphone indicator while the session is on. The keyboard asks for Full Access so it can talk to the app through an App Group and give haptic feedback. It also tells the app what kind of field you are typing in, so the right writing style applies. The app hands the dictated text back to the keyboard in a second file in the folder they share on the same iPhone, and replaces it a few seconds later (if the app is closed at that moment, the text stays there until you open the app again). For Command Mode, the keyboard reads the text you selected, or the last sentence before your cursor if nothing is selected, and passes it to the app through a file in that folder; the next request replaces that file. To keep Undo working, the keyboard also compares the text before your cursor with what it inserted last, only in memory. The keyboard has no network code.
iphone.meetings: Meeting notes on iPhone: you start a recording with the “Record meeting” button and stop it yourself, and the app does not detect meetings by itself. It listens to the microphone only, as one stream with no speaker labels, and transcribes on the iPhone. A phone call or another interruption pauses it. If speech recognition stops working in the middle of a meeting, the app stops the meeting and saves what it heard. While a meeting records, the app listens the whole time and keeps only the words. Starting a meeting ends any running dictation session, so keyboard dictation is off until the meeting ends and you start a new session. Audio is never written to storage. A temporary live journal of the transcript sits in the shared folder and is deleted when the note is saved. If the app is closed in the middle of a meeting or the note cannot be saved, the app turns what is left into a saved note the next time you open it. A summary uses Apple’s on-device model. It needs the “Brain” setting on (it is off by default), Apple Intelligence and enough spoken words. Then it is written by itself when a meeting stops, and a button can write it later if that did not happen. A copy button puts the meeting notes on your clipboard as a ready to paste prompt, so you can paste it into ChatGPT or Claude yourself. iOS may share what you copy with your other Apple devices through Universal Clipboard.
iphone.stored: On iPhone, Speak Away keeps these in a folder that the app and the keyboard share: history (the dictated text, final and original, at most 2,000 entries, on by default; you can turn it off and delete entries one by one), stats that are only counters, your dictionary, voice shortcuts, writing styles, scratchpad, meeting notes and settings. If a data file such as the history cannot be decoded, the app moves it aside as a copy with a .bak ending in the same folder and starts a new one. Speak Away sends none of it anywhere, and there is no account.
control.title: Your control
control.history: Turn history off in the app, or delete entries one by one.
control.folder: To delete stored data on Mac, quit the app first. Save any notes you want to keep elsewhere, then delete ~/Library/Application Support/Speak Away. That folder holds history, dictionary, voice shortcuts, writing styles, scratchpad notes, meeting notes, the downloaded speech model and a small debug log. Stats and settings are in the app’s preferences: run defaults delete com.opensourceeverything.speakaway in Terminal to clear them.
control.uninstall: You can uninstall Speak Away. Its source is available under the MIT license so you can inspect how it handles your data.
children.title: Children
children.text: The same local storage and permissions described here apply when a child uses the app. A parent or guardian can help manage permissions and delete saved data.
changes.title: Changes to this policy
changes.text: If the way Speak Away handles data changes, this page and its update date will change too.
contact.title: Contact
contact.text: Questions about this policy? Open an issue in the project’s GitHub repository.
stored.debug: A small debug log (the last 300 lines) at ~/Library/Application Support/Speak Away/debug.log records key events, action names, how many characters were pasted and errors, never what you dictated.
stored.files: History, meeting notes and the other files are plain files, not encrypted by Speak Away. If the history or another data file is damaged and cannot be read, Speak Away moves it aside as a copy with a .bak ending in the same folder and starts a new one. Deleting entries in the app does not remove that copy; deleting the folder does.
stored.detect: While the app is open, about every five seconds Speak Away checks which apps are running, whether the microphone is in use and, on macOS 14.2 or later, which apps are using it, to offer meeting notes. This stays on your Mac.
permissions.globe: While it runs, Speak Away sets the macOS keyboard option that decides what the Globe key does to “Do Nothing”, so Fn does not open the emoji picker. It puts your value back when you quit normally. If the app closes unexpectedly, the option stays on Do Nothing and you can change it in System Settings › Keyboard. This needs no permission.
